title: THE SIN YOU HATE… AND THE SIN YOU KEEP DEFENDING: JESUS KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE
paragraphs: THE SIN YOU HATE… AND THE SIN YOU KEEP DEFENDING: JESUS KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE

Not everyone who falls into sin has surrendered to it. But not everyone who says “I’m struggling” is actually fighting. There is a difference between a wounded believer reaching for Jesus and a comfortable sinner using grace as permission—and that difference may reveal something about your heart you have been afraid to confront.
There is a prayer God has heard from countless bedrooms, bathroom floors, parked cars, and hospital corridors.
“Lord, I did it again.”
Sometimes those words come through tears.
Sometimes through shame.
Sometimes from someone who genuinely hates what they have done but cannot understand why they keep returning to it.
And sometimes…
Those exact same words come from someone who has already decided they will do it again tomorrow.
Same confession.
Same Bible.
Same church attendance.
Same language about grace.
But something is terribly different beneath the surface.
One person is fighting a sin that keeps knocking them down.
The other has slowly learned to make peace with the very thing Jesus died to deliver them from.
And here is the question that should make every one of us examine our hearts:
Are you struggling against your sin… or struggling to keep your sin while still holding on to Jesus?
Read that again.
Because the answer is not always found in how many times you have fallen.
Sometimes it is found in what you do when the Holy Spirit tells you to get back up.
And before you assume this message is about someone else, remember something.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
Both sinned terribly.
Both experienced remorse.
But their stories did not end the same way.
Peter's story became a testimony of restoration.
Judas's story became a tragedy of despair.

The difference cannot be reduced to the simple claim that one cried harder or felt more guilty. Scripture reveals something much deeper about repentance, faith, mercy, and what happens when a broken person turns toward Christ rather than remaining away from Him.
And somewhere in their stories, we may recognize ourselves.
Maybe you love Jesus.
You genuinely do.
You open your Bible, and something inside you comes alive. You hear worship music, and tears fill your eyes. You remember what Christ suffered on the cross, and you know you owe Him everything.
But then night comes.
The temptation returns.
The phone is in your hand.
The conversation you promised to end begins again.
The bitterness you said you had surrendered rises in your chest.
The pornography you promised never to revisit is one click away.
The lie seems easier than the truth.
The anger feels justified.
The secret relationship still has a place in your heart.
And suddenly, the person who was worshiping God in the morning is wrestling with the same darkness before midnight.
You fall.
And immediately, the accusations begin.
“You are a hypocrite.”
“You never really changed.”
“God must be tired of forgiving you.”
“Real Christians don't struggle like this.”
But listen carefully.
The presence of a battle does not automatically mean the absence of genuine faith.
And the absence of visible guilt does not automatically mean the presence of spiritual maturity.
The Bible is far more honest about the human heart than many of us are willing to be.
The apostle Paul wrote in Galatians 5:17:
“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.” (KJV)
In the original Greek, Paul uses the word ἐπιθυμεῖ (epithymei), meaning “desires” or “longs for.”
The flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit opposes what is contrary to God's will.
Paul is describing real opposition, not peaceful coexistence.
This matters.
Because when someone belongs to Christ, sin is no longer something they should simply accept as their rightful master.
There is conflict.
Conviction.
Resistance.
A growing desire to obey God even when old desires remain powerful.

Yet we must be careful. Feeling conflicted is not, by itself, proof of salvation. People can experience guilt for many reasons. The biblical question is whether we are turning toward Christ in repentance and faith, learning to obey Him through the power of His Spirit.
The struggle is not our Savior.
Jesus is.
And the presence of temptation is not the same as consenting to it.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Think about that.
Our sinless Savior understands temptation without ever surrendering to it.
So being tempted does not make you filthy.
But welcoming temptation, feeding it, protecting it, and deliberately choosing disobedience are not spiritually harmless.
There is a difference between being attacked by temptation and deliberately opening the door to entertain it.
There is a difference between stumbling into sin and arranging your life so that sin is waiting for you.
There is a difference between crying out, “Lord, help me resist,” and whispering, “Lord, forgive me afterward,” while already planning to disobey.
That second prayer should frighten us—not because God's mercy is small, but because we are treating something infinitely precious as though it were cheap.
Paul confronted this thinking directly.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (Romans 6:1–2, KJV)
In Greek, Paul's emphatic response is:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
A forceful rejection.
“Certainly not!”
“May it never be!”
Paul was not merely suggesting that continuing in sin is a bad habit.
He was rejecting the very idea that God's grace gives us permission to remain devoted to the sin from which Christ came to free us.
Grace is not a permission slip to keep walking into darkness.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life in Jesus Christ.
And Titus 2:11–12 tells us that this grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Do you see it?
The same grace that receives a repentant sinner also trains that sinner to turn away from sin.
Grace does not merely comfort us after we fall. It teaches us how to walk differently.
But here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Imagine two people.
Both struggle with lust.
Both have fallen repeatedly.
Both feel ashamed.

One begins removing access to the things that continually lead them into temptation. They confess their struggle to a trustworthy mature believer. They pray even when they feel spiritually exhausted. They seek wise help. They take responsibility. They stop pretending that secrecy is harmless.
They may stumble again.
But they are no longer defending the sin.
They are learning to fight it.
The other person says, “God knows my heart.”
Yet they continue feeding the same desires, hiding the same messages, maintaining the same opportunities, and dismissing every warning.
When confronted, they become defensive.
When Scripture challenges them, they explain it away.
When conviction comes, they silence it with the thought, “Nobody is perfect.”
Both may use the phrase “I'm struggling.”
But the direction of their lives is not the same.

This does not mean genuine repentance always produces instant freedom or uninterrupted progress. Some battles involve addiction, trauma, deeply established habits, or circumstances requiring pastoral, relational, and professional support.
A person can be genuinely repentant and still need sustained help.
But repentance is never meant to become an excuse for refusing help.
The Hebrew word often associated with repentance is שׁוּב (shuv), meaning “to turn” or “return.”
In the Old Testament, this word frequently describes turning away from wrongdoing and returning to the Lord.
God says in Ezekiel 18:30:
“Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin.” (KJV)
The New Testament uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, referring to a change of mind or heart that is expressed in a changed direction of life.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible about what happened.
It is turning toward God with a willingness to leave behind what dishonors Him.
And sometimes that turning begins with trembling hands.
Sometimes it begins with deleting a contact.
Sometimes it begins with confessing a lie.
Sometimes it begins with telling a trusted person, “I need help.”
Sometimes it begins with finally admitting that the thing you keep calling a weakness has become something you are deliberately protecting.
Not every act of repentance feels dramatic.
Sometimes the holiest decision of your day is quietly refusing to return to the place where you know your soul keeps getting wounded.
And perhaps that is why the story of David is so unsettling.
David was not a stranger to God.
He knew worship.
He knew prayer.
He knew the Lord's faithfulness.
Yet in 2 Samuel 11, he committed adultery with Bathsheba, who was married to Uriah, and then orchestrated circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
David's actions were not an innocent mistake.
They were serious, deliberate sins involving terrible abuses of power and devastating harm to others.
And for a time, David concealed what he had done.
Until God sent the prophet Nathan.
Nathan told David a story about injustice.
David became angry at the wickedness in the story.
Then Nathan spoke the words that shattered his defenses:
“Thou art the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7, KJV)
Imagine that moment.
The king who could command armies could not command the truth to disappear.
The man who had concealed his wrongdoing stood exposed before the God who had seen everything.
And David finally said:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
No elaborate defense.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No claim that being king made him exempt.
No attempt to rename evil as weakness.
David confessed.
Psalm 51 gives us a profound picture of his repentance.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from bara, meaning “to create.”
David was asking God for something deeper than improved appearances.
He needed inward renewal.
He needed mercy.
He needed a heart transformed by the Lord.
And notice something else.
David's forgiveness did not erase the earthly consequences of his actions.
The biblical account records painful consequences that followed.
Forgiveness is real.
Consequences can also be real.
Grace does not mean that sin was never serious, that victims were never harmed, or that accountability is unnecessary.
It means that God can show mercy to sinners without calling their evil good.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to manage your image while your heart remains exhausted.
People see the smile.
God sees the secret.
People hear the worship.
God hears the private negotiations you make with temptation.
People see the Bible verse on your profile.
God knows whether you are surrendering to the truth behind it.
And still, He calls sinners to repent.
Not because He delights in crushing broken people.
But because the sin we refuse to surrender can become the very thing that destroys us.
Now consider Peter.
The night Jesus was arrested, Peter insisted that he would remain faithful.
He sounded courageous.
Certain.
Ready to suffer.
But when pressure came, Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 records one of the most heartbreaking moments in Scripture:
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
Just imagine.
The rooster had crowed.
The words of Jesus came rushing back.
And Peter realized what he had done.
Luke tells us that he went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's tears were not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in John 21.
Three times Jesus asked Peter whether he loved Him, and He entrusted Peter with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied knowing Jesus was called again to serve Him.
Not because Peter's denial was insignificant.
Not because Peter had earned another chance through tears.
But because the risen Christ is merciful and powerful to restore.
And perhaps you need to hear this:
Your worst failure does not have to become the final chapter of your life.
The cross is not too weak to deal with your sin.
The resurrection is not too small to give you hope.
The mercy of Jesus is not exhausted because you are ashamed to come before Him again.
But do not confuse restoration with permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not restore Peter so that Peter could celebrate his denial.
He restored him to love, obedience, and service.
And this is where the Gospel becomes both deeply comforting and deeply confronting.
Jesus does not demand that you clean yourself up before you are allowed to come to Him.
He calls you to come to Him in repentance and faith.
But the Jesus who welcomes sinners also calls them to follow Him.
In John 8, after the woman accused of adultery was brought before Jesus, He refused to join in her condemnation by her accusers.
Then He said:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy and holiness were not enemies in His words.
He did not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
He did not say, “You must become flawless before I will show compassion.”
He extended mercy and called her away from sin.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not condemnation without hope.
Not acceptance without transformation.
But salvation through Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners and calls those He saves into a new life.
And there is a warning we cannot ignore.
Hebrews 10:26 speaks seriously about willful sin after receiving the knowledge of the truth.
The surrounding passage warns against a settled, defiant rejection of Christ and His sacrifice.
This is not a declaration that every believer who knowingly sins has become permanently unforgivable.
If that were the case, the biblical calls to confession, repentance, restoration, and perseverance would make little sense.
But it is a terrifying warning against treating the Son of God with contempt while presuming that His sacrifice can be rejected without consequence.
Do not use this passage to crush a repentant person who desperately wants to return to Jesus.
And do not use the promises of grace to reassure someone who is determined to reject Him.
Both mistakes distort Scripture.
First John 1:8 says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Then verse 9 gives this beautiful promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And First John 2:1 says:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”
Do not miss the balance.
John writes so that believers will not sin.
But when they do sin, he points them to Jesus Christ, their righteous Advocate.
Not to excuses.
Not to despair.
To Jesus.

And First John 3 also warns against making sin one's continuing practice. John's point is not that Christians achieve sinless perfection in this life, but that a life characterized by allegiance to sin contradicts the new life God gives.
So how do you know whether you are struggling with sin or choosing to live in it?
You cannot settle that question by counting your tears.
You cannot settle it by comparing yourself to another Christian.
You cannot settle it by demanding that you never experience temptation again.
Instead, bring your heart honestly before the Lord.
When Scripture exposes your sin, do you submit to its truth or search for a way around it?
When you fall, do you confess and seek help, or immediately begin planning how to hide it?
Are you willing to remove the opportunities that repeatedly lead you into disobedience?
Do you want freedom from sin itself, or only freedom from the consequences of being discovered?
When someone lovingly confronts you, can you receive correction?
And perhaps the most revealing question of all:
If nobody ever found out, would you still want to stop because you love Jesus?
Sit with that.
Not because one answer can perfectly measure the state of your soul.
Only God knows the heart completely.
But because honest self-examination can expose what pride has been protecting.
Second Corinthians 13:5 calls believers to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith.
That examination is not meant to replace trust in Christ with endless obsession over ourselves.
It is meant to turn us away from false confidence and toward genuine faith.
Because salvation is not earned by winning enough battles against temptation.
Ephesians 2:8–9 tells us that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And verse 10 reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase salvation.
It is part of the fruit God produces in the lives of those who belong to Christ.
We do not fight sin to convince Jesus to love us.
We fight sin because His love has reached us, and His Spirit is at work within us.
Philippians 2:12–13 calls believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling because God Himself works in them both to will and to do His good pleasure.
That means you are not called to fight by your own strength alone.
You need the Word.
You need prayer.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need the fellowship of believers.
You may need accountability, pastoral care, counseling, or practical changes to your environment.
And when your sin has harmed another person, repentance may require truthfulness, restitution where possible, and accepting appropriate consequences.
Forgiveness is never a license to continue hurting people.
But perhaps the greatest danger is not that you have struggled for a long time.
Perhaps it is that you have slowly stopped believing freedom is worth pursuing.
You have begun calling bondage your personality.
You have begun calling compromise your situation.
You have begun calling deliberate disobedience your weakness.
You have become so accustomed to apologizing for the same behavior that you no longer seriously consider turning away from it.
And the saddest part?
You may still know how to sound spiritual.
You can quote Scripture.
You can say “God is good.”
You can lift your hands during worship.
You can encourage someone else to trust Jesus.
All while keeping a private corner of your life where His authority is unwelcome.
But Jesus did not die merely to become a comforting addition to a life we refuse to surrender.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to break the dominion of sin and give His people new life.
Romans 6:14 declares:
“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
The word translated “have dominion” comes from the Greek verb κυριεύω (kyrieuō), meaning to rule or exercise mastery.
Paul is speaking about sin's mastery.
And this is the hope of every believer who feels trapped.
You may still face temptation.
You may still need to repent.
You may still need to fight old patterns with serious, sustained effort.
But sin does not have to be your rightful ruler.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And He is worthy of more than the parts of your life you find convenient to surrender.
Maybe right now the Holy Spirit is bringing something specific to your attention.
A secret.
A relationship.
A habit.
An attitude.
An unforgiving heart.
A dishonest practice.
Something you have explained away for years.
Do not turn this moment into another performance.
You do not need to type a dramatic confession to prove that you are serious.
You do not need to tell the entire internet your private struggles.
But you do need to be honest before God.
And if you are able, find a trustworthy mature Christian who can pray with you, encourage you, and help you take meaningful steps toward obedience.
James 5:16 speaks of confessing faults to one another and praying for one another.
There is strength in refusing to fight every battle alone.
You do not have to expose personal details.
Someone reading those words may realize that repentance is not the end of hope.
It may be the beginning of coming home.
Remember the prodigal son.
He did not return to his father carrying a record of achievements.
He returned knowing he had sinned.
He had wasted what was entrusted to him.
He had reached a place of humiliation and need.
But Luke 15:20 says that while he was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran, embraced him, and kissed him.
Jesus told that parable to reveal the extraordinary joy associated with the repentance of sinners.
The son did not earn his welcome by pretending he had never rebelled.
He came home.
And the father's compassion did not mean rebellion had been good.
It meant mercy was greater than the son's ability to repair his own disgrace.
Maybe you have been living far from the Father while still knowing all the songs sung in His house.
Maybe you have been pretending that everything is fine.
Maybe you have been struggling sincerely and have mistaken your ongoing battle for proof that God has abandoned you.
Hear the Gospel again.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures. (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)
This is not merely a message about becoming a more disciplined person.
It is the announcement of what Jesus has accomplished for sinners.
The innocent Savior bore sin.
The crucified King rose victorious.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds a Savior who is able to forgive and transform.
Your shame cannot save you.
Your promises cannot save you.
Your religious image cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ can save you.
So stop trying to negotiate with the sin that is destroying your peace.
Stop telling yourself you will repent someday when the temptation becomes less attractive.
Stop confusing the patience of God with His approval of your disobedience.
And if you are the exhausted believer who has been fighting, falling, confessing, and getting back up, do not surrender to despair.
Keep coming to Christ.
Keep walking in the light.
Keep seeking help.
Keep taking the next faithful step.
Your struggle is not something to celebrate.
But neither is it a reason to abandon the only Savior who can deliver you.
There is still hope for the repentant.
There is still mercy at the cross.
There is still power in the risen Jesus.
And there is still a calling to walk in the newness of life He gives.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending to be perfect.
Not to make Christianity look impressive from the outside while hearts quietly starve.

But to keep pointing people toward the Word of God, the truth of the Gospel, genuine repentance, the sufficiency of Christ, and a life of discipleship that continues long after an emotional moment has passed.
Because sometimes a single article reaches someone who has not opened a Bible in years.
Sometimes a Scripture shared on Facebook reaches a person who would never walk into a church voluntarily.
Sometimes a message of repentance reaches someone just before they make another destructive decision.
And sometimes a testimony of grace reminds a wounded believer that returning to Jesus is still possible.
Not because sharing earns God's favor.
Not because the number of reactions measures spiritual fruit.
But because the truth of Scripture deserves to be heard, and sharing it may place this message before someone who needs encouragement or correction.
We want this to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, where grace is never cheapened, and where hurting people are continually directed to Jesus Christ.
It is an opportunity to give generously toward work you believe honors Christ.
But I want to make something biblically clear.
You do not have to pay us to prove your love for Jesus.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
These items are simply an expression of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and they cannot purchase the favor of God.
But if God has given you both the desire and the means to help sustain this work, we would be grateful to have you walking alongside us.
Pray for us.
Share biblical truth.
Encourage another believer.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
Point a wandering soul back toward the Savior.
The Kingdom of God is not built by treating people as transactions.
Our calling is faithfulness to Christ.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you one final question.
Not about someone else's sin.
Not about the person who betrayed you.
Not about the believer whose hypocrisy makes you angry.
About you.
What is the one thing you keep asking Jesus to forgive, while still refusing to surrender it to Him?
You do not have to answer publicly.
But please answer honestly before God.
And if your answer reveals a place where you have been deliberately choosing sin, do not respond with hopelessness.
Respond with repentance.
Turn toward Christ.
Confess what is true.
Receive His mercy by faith.
Take the practical steps that obedience requires.

And if your answer reveals a battle you have been genuinely fighting, remember that the Savior who calls you to holiness also invites you to draw near for mercy and grace in your time of need. (Hebrews 4:16)
You are not saved because you have never fallen.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves also calls you into a transformed life.

So tonight, whether you are kneeling beside your bed, sitting alone in your car, staring at a phone you need to put away, or holding back tears in a room where nobody knows what you are facing, remember this.
You can stop defending the darkness.
You can come into the light.
You can stop pretending.
You can confess.
You can seek help.
You can turn again toward Jesus.
Because the question is not whether your past contains a scandal.
Every one of us has sinned and fallen short of the glory of God.
The question is whether you will bring your sin to the Savior who alone can forgive and make you new.
And if there is one thing I pray you remember long after this article disappears from your screen, it is this:
The most dangerous place is not the floor where a repentant sinner falls to their knees—it is the comfortable darkness where a heart no longer wants to come home.
